    \item \good{One clean win: a free error bar.} $\langle Q\rangle_W-\langle Q\rangle_U$ is
          \emph{exactly} zero by conservation, so its measured value is device error

  \end{itemize}

% ==================================================================
\section{The question}

\begin{frame}{You compiled $U$ into something cheaper. Is it still right?}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.56\textwidth}
      Every practical quantum simulation replaces the target evolution $U(t)$ with a cheaper
      approximation $W$ --- a Trotter product formula, a transpiler setting, or an
      \hl{AQC-compressed ansatz}.
      \medskip

      The question that decides whether the result means anything:
      \begin{center}\bad{how wrong is $W$, and wrong in \emph{what}?}\end{center}
      \medskip

      Classically you answer it by simulating both. That is exactly the thing you cannot do
      at the sizes where you need the answer.
      \medskip

      \textbf{Track B} answers it \emph{on the device}: put $W$ on one ancilla branch and
      $U$ on the other, and the interference is the overlap of two dynamics.
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}
      \centering
      \vspace{4mm}
      \fbox{\parbox{0.95\linewidth}{\centering\small\vspace{1mm}
      $W$ = what you can afford to run\\[2mm]
      $U$ = what you meant to run\\[3mm]
      \hl{$\chi_{AB}(t)=\langle\psi|W^\dagger U|\psi\rangle$}\\[1mm]
      {\footnotesize measured, not simulated}
      \vspace{1mm}}}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
\end{frame}

% ==================================================================
\section{The instrument}

\begin{frame}{Anti-control: how the Hadamard test is extended}
  \vspace{-1mm}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=0.93\linewidth]{fig_tb_anticontrol.png}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-2mm}
  {\footnotesize The only structural change is the $X$--$cW$--$X$ sandwich: it makes $W$ fire
  on the $|0\rangle$ branch, so the ancilla interferes \hl{two dynamics} rather than one
  against the identity. Everything downstream is unchanged. Algebra in appendix A1--A2.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Track B: anti-controlled Hadamard test}
  \small
  Replace controlled-$U$ with ``$W$ when the ancilla is $|0\rangle$, $U$ when it is
  $|1\rangle$''. Then, with the \emph{same} quadrature convention as the ordinary test,
  \[
    \langle Z_a\rangle_\phi=\mathrm{Re}\!\left[e^{i\phi}\langle\psi|W^\dagger U|\psi\rangle
    \right],\qquad \phi=0\to\mathrm{Re}\,\chi_{AB},\quad
    \phi=-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\to\mathrm{Im}\,\chi_{AB}
  \]
  Setting $W=\mathbb{1}$ recovers the ordinary Hadamard test exactly, so this is a strict
  generalisation --- which also means it needs \emph{its own} validation, not inherited trust.
  \medskip

  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{lr}
    \toprule
    statevector identity, frozen 3-site (3 times $\times$ 2 reps $\times$ 2 quadratures)
      & \good{$8.99\times10^{-15}$} \src{R034}\\
    statevector identity, 2-site (4 times $\times$ 2 reps $\times$ 2 quadratures)
      & \good{$4.56\times10^{-15}$} \src{R042}\\
    $\chi_{AB}(0)=1$ exactly, as it must be (both branches are the identity) & \good{yes}\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  \medskip

  {\footnotesize\color{orangeA}\textbf{A bug this caught.} Our first reference took the
  $|1\rangle$-control block as the \emph{upper half} of the gate matrix. The notebook builds
  the gate with the ancilla as its \emph{lowest} bit, so the block is the odd sublattice.
  The wrong version passes at $t=0$ --- where both branches are the identity --- and fails
  everywhere else. It was caught before any QPU time was spent.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{First, what a classical shadow is}
  \vspace{-1mm}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=0.90\linewidth]{fig_shadow.png}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-2mm}
  {\footnotesize
  In Track B this is applied to the \emph{system} register --- the one a standard Hadamard
  test throws away. It costs \hl{no new circuits}, and it makes one record set an unbiased
  estimator for \hl{every} Pauli at once. {\color{mutedA}(Schematic uses 3 qubits; our
  Track B instance has 2.)} \src{Huang, Kueng \& Preskill, \emph{Nat.\ Phys.}
  \textbf{16}, 1050 (2020); proof in A4}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{What the shadows add: delete the final Hadamard}
  \small
  Before the final Hadamard the state is
  $\bigl(|0\rangle W|\psi\rangle+e^{i\phi}|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle\bigr)/\sqrt2$. Tracing the
  ancilla out of the \emph{un-Hadamarded} circuit gives two different things at once:
  \[
    \mathrm{tr}_a\bigl[\rho_{\text{out}}\bigr]=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(W\rho W^\dagger+U\rho U^\dagger\bigr),
    \qquad
    \mathrm{tr}_a\bigl[(Z\otimes\mathbb{1})\rho_{\text{out}}\bigr]
      =\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(W\rho W^\dagger-U\rho U^\dagger\bigr)
  \]
  Both are \emph{independent of $\phi$}, so one quadrature suffices. Add and subtract:
  \begin{center}
  \hl{$\langle O\rangle_W$ and $\langle O\rangle_U$ separately, for every Pauli $O$,
  from one family of circuits.}
  \end{center}
  \medskip

  That is the \emph{per-observable disagreement profile} --- the part of Track B the
  scaffold flags and that our own R034 explicitly did \bad{not} deliver. Validated to
  \good{$4.44\times10^{-15}$} across 4 times $\times$ 6 observables before submission.
  \src{R042}
  \medskip

  \centering\textbf{The ancilla says \emph{how much} $W$ is wrong. The garbage says
  \emph{which observable}.}
\end{frame}

\section{Against the baselines that already exist}

\begin{frame}{We are not the only way to do this --- and not the cheapest}
  \vspace{-1mm}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=0.99\linewidth]{fig_tb_baselines.png}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-2mm}
  {\footnotesize
  \textbf{Loschmidt echo}: prepare, apply $U$, apply $W^\dagger$, un-prepare, read the
  all-zeros probability. \textbf{Hilbert--Schmidt test} (Khatri \emph{et al.},
  \emph{Quantum} \textbf{3}, 140 (2019)): Bell pairs on $2n$ qubits give the
  \emph{state-independent} $|\mathrm{Tr}[W^\dagger U]/d|^2$. Both verified against exact
  values before being used as baselines. \src{R043}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The honest scoreboard}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{lccccc}
    \toprule
    & \textbf{qubits} & \textbf{2q gates} & \textbf{phase?} & \textbf{state-indep.?}
      & \textbf{which observable?}\\
    \midrule
    classical fidelity {\tiny(AQC's own score)} & --- & --- & n/a & yes & no\\
    Loschmidt echo        & $n$   & \good{2}  & no  & no  & no\\
    Hilbert--Schmidt test & $2n$  & 16        & no  & \good{yes} & no\\
    Track B, ancilla only & $n{+}1$ & 136     & \good{yes} & no & no\\
    Track B $+$ shadows {\tiny(ours)} & $n{+}1$ & 136 & \good{yes} & no & \good{yes}\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  \smallskip
  \small
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \bad{The echo is cheaper than us at every $n$ we measured} --- $6.0\times$ at
          $n{=}3$ and $4.0\times$ at $n{=}4$. If all you want is a scalar ``how close is
          $W$ to $U$'', \emph{use the echo}. \src{R043}
    \item The $52\times$ gap at $n{=}2$ is a \emph{unitary-collapse artefact} (any product of
          2-qubit unitaries fuses into one). We quote 4--6$\times$, never 52$\times$.
    \item The HST answers a \emph{stronger} question than either overlap, and costs $2n$
          qubits for it.
  \end{itemize}
  \centering\textbf{Our arm has to be justified by what it returns, never by being cheaper.}
\end{frame}

% ==================================================================
\section{AQC: the compressor and its certificate}

\begin{frame}{AQC compression, certified by our own Track-B observable}
  \small
  Approximate Quantum Compiling (\texttt{qiskit-addon-aqc-tensor}, quimb$+$jax MPS backend)
  optimises a shallow ansatz against an MPS target. It scores itself with a
  \emph{classical} fidelity --- the one number you lose access to at scale.
  \medskip

  \begin{center}
  Set $W=$ the AQC circuit and $U=$ exact: then
  \hl{$\chi_{AB}=\langle\psi|W^\dagger U|\psi\rangle$ \emph{is} the compression fidelity},
  measured from shots.
  \end{center}
  \medskip

  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{lccc}
    \toprule
    & \textbf{Trotter} & \textbf{exact synth.} & \textbf{AQC}\\
    \midrule
    \emph{uncontrolled} $n{=}3$ (infid. $1.4\!\times\!10^{-4}$) & 68 & 19 & \good{9}\\
    \emph{uncontrolled} $n{=}4$ (infid. $2.6\!\times\!10^{-4}$) & 104 & 95 & \good{15}\\
    \midrule
    \emph{controlled} $n{=}3$ --- what a Hadamard test runs & --- & \good{50} & \bad{132}\\
    \emph{controlled} $n{=}4$ & --- & 236 & \good{216}\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  \smallskip
  {\footnotesize The compressor and the certificate come from two different halves of this
  project. \bad{But the story reverses under control:} at $n{=}3$ AQC is $2.6\times$
  \emph{worse}, because controlling an ansatz pays overhead on every gate while the direct
  block construction pays none. Crossover sits at $n\!\sim\!4$. \src{R035}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The garbage also ships a free error bar}
  \label{slide:freebar}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.54\textwidth}
      \centering
      \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_tb_symmetry.png}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.44\textwidth}
      \small
      $Q=\sum_j Z_j$ commutes with $H$, and \emph{every} Trotter factor conserves it --- so
      $\langle Q\rangle_W-\langle Q\rangle_U$ is \hl{exactly zero} for any $W$ in this family.
      \medskip

      Measured: $-0.04$, $-0.39$, $-0.25$, $-0.34$. \src{R044}
      \medskip

      That deviation is \good{pure device error, detected with no reference state, no exact
      diagonalisation and no simulation} --- and it correctly flags the same times where the
      other observables went bad.
      \medskip

      {\footnotesize\color{mutedA} It is a diagnostic, not a correction: we do \emph{not}
      post-select on it, which would bias the shadow estimators.}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
\end{frame}

\section{What we claim}

\begin{frame}{What we claim, and what we do not}
  \small
  \textbf{We claim}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Track B \hl{completed}: the per-observable disagreement profile via the X-basis
          readout, which our own R034 left undone. Identity validated to $4\times10^{-15}$
          on two models. \src{R042}
    \item An AQC-compressed circuit \hl{certified by a shot-based observable} rather than a
          classical fidelity --- the certificate survives to sizes where the classical score
          does not. \src{R035}
    \item Track B run on a \hl{QPU for the first time in this project}, against two
          literature baselines in the same job. \src{R044}
  \end{itemize}
  \medskip
  \textbf{We do not claim}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \bad{That our method is the best way to get the scalar overlap.} It is not --- the
          Loschmidt echo is 4--6$\times$ cheaper and, on hardware, markedly more accurate.
    \item \bad{That AQC helps a Hadamard test at these sizes.} Under control it is
          $2.6\times$ worse at $n{=}3$; the crossover is at $n\!\sim\!4$. \src{R035}
    \item Any advantage over classical computation. The instance is 2--3 qubits and a laptop
          solves it exactly --- which is the point: every number here is graded against truth.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Future work: the same circuit is a density-of-states estimator}
  \label{slide:dos}
  \vspace{-1mm}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=0.93\linewidth]{fig_tb_dos.png}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-2mm}
  {\footnotesize
  Feed Track B the \hl{maximally mixed} state instead of $|\psi\rangle$ and the ancilla
  measures $\mathrm{Tr}[W^{\dagger}U]/d$. With $W=I$ that is
  $\mathrm{Tr}[U(t)]/d$ --- the generating function whose Fourier transform is the
  \hl{density of states}, i.e.\ Eq.~(7) of Goh \& Koczor (arXiv:2407.03414v2). So their DOS
  protocol is the $W{=}I$ special case of our Track B circuit, not a separate experiment.
  Verified to $2.2\times10^{-15}$; measured on the simulator at rms $0.0085$ and $0.0072$.
  \src{R045}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[plain]
  \centering\Large\textbf{Appendix --- derivations}\\[1em]
  {\normalsize\color{mutedA} A1 anti-control \quad A2 the Track B identity \quad
  A3 the two readouts\\ A4 classical shadows \quad A5 shadows on the Track B circuit}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A1 --- Anti-control, and A2 --- the Track B identity}
  \small
  \textbf{A1.} A controlled gate fires on $|1\rangle$. Conjugating the ancilla by $X$ swaps
  the two branches:
  \[
    X_a\Bigl(|0\rangle\!\langle0|\otimes\mathbb{1}+|1\rangle\!\langle1|\otimes W\Bigr)X_a
    \;=\;|1\rangle\!\langle1|\otimes\mathbb{1}+|0\rangle\!\langle0|\otimes W
  \]
  so $X\!-\!cW\!-\!X$ applies $W$ exactly when the ancilla is $|0\rangle$. Composing it with
  an ordinary $cU$ puts a \emph{different} evolution on each branch.
  \medskip

  \textbf{A2.} Propagating $|0\rangle_a|\psi\rangle$ through the circuit:
  \[
    \xrightarrow{\;H\;}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)|\psi\rangle
    \xrightarrow{\;X cW X\;}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(|0\rangle W|\psi\rangle+|1\rangle|\psi\rangle\bigr)
    \xrightarrow{\;cU\;}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(|0\rangle W|\psi\rangle+|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle\bigr)
  \]
  \[
    \xrightarrow{\;P(\phi)\;}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(|0\rangle W|\psi\rangle+e^{i\phi}|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle\bigr)
    \xrightarrow{\;H\;}\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[|0\rangle(W+e^{i\phi}U)|\psi\rangle+|1\rangle(W-e^{i\phi}U)|\psi\rangle\Bigr]
  \]
  Using $\bigl\|(W\pm e^{i\phi}U)\psi\bigr\|^{2}=2\pm2\,\mathrm{Re}\bigl[e^{i\phi}\langle\psi|W^\dagger U|\psi\rangle\bigr]$,
  \[
    \langle Z_a\rangle_\phi=\tfrac{1}{4}\Bigl(\bigl\|(W+e^{i\phi}U)\psi\bigr\|^{2}
    -\bigl\|(W-e^{i\phi}U)\psi\bigr\|^{2}\Bigr)
    =\mathrm{Re}\!\left[e^{i\phi}\langle\psi|W^{\dagger}U|\psi\rangle\right]
  \]
  \centering $W=\mathbb{1}$ returns the standard test, so this is a strict generalisation.
  \src{verified numerically to $4.56\times10^{-15}$, R042}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A3 --- the two readouts: why deleting one gate gives the difference}
  \small
  Stop \emph{before} the final Hadamard. With
  $|\Phi\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(|0\rangle W|\psi\rangle+e^{i\phi}|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle\bigr)$
  and $\rho=|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi|$,
  \[
    \rho_{\text{out}}=|\Phi\rangle\!\langle\Phi|=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[
      |0\rangle\!\langle0|\otimes W\rho W^{\dagger}
    + |1\rangle\!\langle1|\otimes U\rho U^{\dagger}
    + e^{-i\phi}|0\rangle\!\langle1|\otimes W\rho U^{\dagger}
    + \text{h.c.}\Bigr]
  \]
  The off-diagonal ancilla blocks are killed by both partial traces below, so \emph{both
  results are independent of $\phi$} --- one quadrature suffices:
  \[
    \mathrm{tr}_a\bigl[\rho_{\text{out}}\bigr]=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(W\rho W^{\dagger}+U\rho U^{\dagger}\bigr)
    \equiv S,
    \qquad
    \mathrm{tr}_a\bigl[(Z\otimes\mathbb{1})\rho_{\text{out}}\bigr]
      =\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(W\rho W^{\dagger}-U\rho U^{\dagger}\bigr)\equiv D
  \]
  Hence for \emph{any} observable $O$, from the same shots,
  \[
    \langle O\rangle_W=\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[O(S+D)\bigr],\qquad
    \langle O\rangle_U=\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[O(S-D)\bigr]
  \]
  \centering\textbf{Keeping the final $H$ gives the overlap; deleting it gives the
  per-observable profile.}
  \src{verified to $4.44\times10^{-15}$ over 4 times $\times$ 6 observables, R042}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A4 --- classical shadows: the inversion and its variance}
  \small
  Measure each qubit in a basis $b_j$ drawn uniformly from $\{X,Y,Z\}$, with
  $V_bWV_b^{\dagger}=Z$. The single-qubit measurement channel is
  \[
    \mathcal{M}_1(\sigma)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{b,s}\Bigl[\langle s|V_b\sigma V_b^{\dagger}|s\rangle\,
      V_b^{\dagger}|s\rangle\!\langle s|V_b\Bigr]
    =\tfrac{1}{3}\sigma+\tfrac{1}{3}\mathrm{Tr}(\sigma)\,\mathbb{1}
  \]
  --- expand $\sigma$ over $\{\mathbb{1},X,Y,Z\}$: the identity part always survives, and each
  traceless part survives only when \emph{its own} basis is drawn, with probability $1/3$.
  Inverting on the traceless part,
  \[
    \mathcal{M}_1^{-1}(A)=3A-\mathrm{Tr}(A)\,\mathbb{1}
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \hat\rho=\bigotimes_j\Bigl(3\,V_{b_j}^{\dagger}|s_j\rangle\!\langle s_j|V_{b_j}-\mathbb{1}\Bigr),
    \qquad \mathbb{E}[\hat\rho]=\rho
  \]
  For a Pauli string $P$, the single-qubit traces are $1$ ($P_j=\mathbb{1}$), $3s_j$
  ($P_j=b_j$), and $0$ otherwise, so
  \[
    \hat P=3^{\,w(P)}\!\!\prod_{j\in\mathrm{supp}(P)}\!\! s_j\,\mathbf{1}\bigl[b_j=P_j\bigr],
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat P^{2}\bigr]=3^{2w}\cdot\underbrace{3^{-w}}_{\text{all }w\text{ match}}=3^{\,w(P)}
  \]
  \centering The second moment is \hl{exactly $3^{w}$}, independent of $\rho$ --- which is why
  low-weight observables are cheap and weight-$n$ ones are not. \src{HKP, \emph{Nat.\ Phys.}
  \textbf{16}, 1050 (2020); CONVENTIONS \S(Pauli-string estimator)}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A5 --- putting them together on the Track B circuit}
  \small
  Each shot of arm B records $(b_0\ldots b_{n-1},\,s_0\ldots s_{n-1},\,a)$ with $a=\pm1$ the
  ancilla outcome. Form $\hat P$ from the system record as in A4. Then, by A3,
  \[
    \mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat P\bigr]=\mathrm{Tr}[P\,S]=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\langle P\rangle_W+\langle P\rangle_U\bigr),
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}\bigl[a\,\hat P\bigr]=\mathrm{Tr}[P\,D]=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\langle P\rangle_W-\langle P\rangle_U\bigr)
  \]
  so a single sample mean of each gives both dynamics separately, for every $P$ at once:
  \[
    \widehat{\langle P\rangle_W}=\overline{\hat P}+\overline{a\hat P},
    \qquad
    \widehat{\langle P\rangle_U}=\overline{\hat P}-\overline{a\hat P}
  \]
  \medskip
  \textbf{Two consequences we use on the slides.}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Any $O=\sum_P c_P P$ follows by linearity --- $H$, $Q$, and the hopping term all
          come from the same records.
    \item If $[O,H]=0$ and every factor of $W$ conserves $O$, then
          $\langle O\rangle_W-\langle O\rangle_U\equiv0$ \emph{identically}. Its measured
          value is therefore \hl{pure device error}, with no reference needed --- the free
          error bar on slide~\ref{slide:freebar}. \src{R044}
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A6 --- Track B $\to$ density of states, and where the phase matters}
  \small
  With $\rho=\mathbb{1}/d$ the Track B identity of A2 becomes state-\emph{independent}:
  \[
    \chi_{AB}(t)=\mathrm{Tr}\!\left[W^{\dagger}U\rho\right]
    \;\xrightarrow{\;\rho=\mathbb{1}/d\;}\;
    \frac{1}{d}\mathrm{Tr}\!\left[W^{\dagger}U\right]
    \qquad\text{and at }W=\mathbb{1}:\quad \frac{1}{d}\mathrm{Tr}\!\left[U(t)\right]
  \]
  which is Eq.~(7) of Goh \& Koczor up to normalisation. Since
  $\mathrm{Tr}[A]=\sum_z\langle z|A|z\rangle$, the mixed input is realised by enumerating the
  $d$ computational basis states --- the deterministic version of their Statement 2 (a
  1-design, e.g.\ random $\{\mathbb{1},X\}^{\otimes n}$, suffices).
  \medskip

  \textbf{Where the phase is worth having --- measured, not assumed:}
  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{lcc}
    \toprule
    & $\max|\mathrm{Im}|$ & does the HST lose information?\\
    \midrule
    $W=\mathbb{1}$ (the DOS signal) & \good{0.504} & \good{yes} --- it returns magnitude only\\
    $W=$ 2nd-order Suzuki (Trotter error) & \bad{$2.8\times10^{-14}$} & \bad{no} --- it is real anyway\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  \smallskip
  {\footnotesize Real $H$ gives $U^{*}=U^{\dagger}$, and a \emph{palindromic} product formula
  gives $W^{*}=W^{\dagger}$, which forces $\mathrm{Tr}[W^{\dagger}U]$ real. So our advantage
  over the HST is the full complex value \emph{for the DOS case}, and only the register size
  ($n{+}1$ vs $2n$) for the Trotter case. \bad{We checked this rather than claiming the phase
  everywhere.} A measured nonzero $\mathrm{Im}$ in the second row is therefore another
  reference-free error signal. \src{R045}}
\end{frame}
